{{Short description|Function in fluid mathematics}}
{{technical|date=June 2014}}

'''Monin–Obukhov (M–O) similarity theory''' describes the non-dimensionalized mean flow and mean temperature in the [[surface layer]] under non-neutral conditions as a function of the dimensionless height parameter,<ref name=mo54>{{cite journal|last=Monin|first=A. S.|author2=Obukhov, A. M.|title=Basic laws of turbulent mixing in the surface layer of the atmosphere|journal=Tr. Akad. Nauk. SSSR Geophiz. Inst.|date=1954|volume=24|issue=151|pages=163–187}}</ref> named after Russian scientists [[Andrei Monin|A. S. Monin]] and [[Alexander Obukhov|A. M. Obukhov]]. [[Similarity theory]] is an empirical method that describes universal relationships between non-dimensionalized variables of fluids based on the [[Buckingham π theorem]]. Similarity theory is extensively used in boundary layer meteorology since relations in turbulent processes are not always resolvable from first principles.<ref name=s88>{{cite book|last=Stull|first=Roland|title=An introduction to boundary layer meteorology|date=1988|publisher=Springer|location=Netherlands|isbn=978-94-009-3027-8}}</ref>

An idealized vertical profile of the mean flow for a neutral boundary layer is the [[logarithmic wind profile]] derived from [[Ludwig Prandtl|Prandtl]]'s [[Mixing length model|mixing length theory]],<ref name=p25>{{cite journal|last=Prandtl|first=Ludwig|title=Bericht über Untersuchungen zur ausgebildeten Turbulenz|journal=Zeitschrift für Angewandte Mathematik und Mechanik|year=1925|volume=5|issue=2|pages=136–139|doi=10.1002/zamm.19250050212|bibcode=1925ZaMM....5..136P|hdl=2060/20050029454|hdl-access=free}}</ref> which states that the horizontal component of mean flow is proportional to the logarithm of height. M–O similarity theory further generalizes the mixing length theory in non-neutral conditions by using so-called "universal functions" of dimensionless height to characterize vertical distributions of mean flow and temperature. The Obukhov length (<math>L</math>), a [[characteristic length]] scale of surface layer turbulence derived by Obukhov in 1946,<ref name=o71/> is used for non-dimensional scaling of the actual height. M–O similarity theory marked a significant landmark of modern [[Microscale meteorology|micrometeorology]], providing a theoretical basis for micrometeorological experiments and measurement techniques.<ref name=f06>{{cite journal|last=Foken|first=T.|title=50 Years of the Monin-Obukhov similarity theory|journal=Boundary-Layer Meteorology|year=2006|volume=2|issue=3|pages=7–29|doi=10.1007/s10546-006-9048-6|bibcode=2006BoLMe.119..431F|s2cid=122060208 }}</ref>

== The Obukhov length ==
The Obukhov length <math>L</math> is a length parameter for the surface layer in the [[boundary layer]], which characterizes the relative contributions to [[Turbulence kinetic energy|turbulent kinetic energy]] from buoyant production and shear production. The Obukhov length was formulated using Richardson's criterion for dynamic stability.<ref name=o71>{{cite journal|last=Obukhov|first=A. M.|title=Turbulence in an atmosphere with a non-uniform temperature|journal=Boundary-Layer Meteorology|date=1971|volume=2|issue=1|pages=7–29|doi=10.1007/BF00718085|bibcode = 1971BoLMe...2....7O |s2cid=121123105 }}</ref> It was derived as,

:<math>
L=-\dfrac{u_*^3}{\kappa \dfrac{g}{T}\dfrac{Q}{\rho c_p}}
</math>

where <math>\kappa\approx 0.40</math> is the [[von Kármán constant]], <math>u_*</math> [[Shear velocity|friction velocity]], <math>Q</math> turbulent [[heat flux]], and <math>c_p</math> [[heat capacity]].<ref name=o71 />  Virtual [[potential temperature]] <math>\theta_v</math> is often used instead of temperature <math>T</math> to correct for the effects of pressure and [[water vapor]]. <math>Q</math> can be written as vertical eddy flux,

:<math>
Q=\rho c_p \overline{w'\theta_v'}
</math>

with <math>w'</math> and <math>\theta_v'</math> perturbations of vertical velocity and virtual potential temperature, respectively. Therefore, the Obukhov length can also be defined as,<ref name=f08>{{cite book|last=Foken|first=Thomas|title=Micrometeorology|url=https://archive.org/details/micrometeorology00foke|url-access=limited|date=2008|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-3-540-74665-2|pages=[https://archive.org/details/micrometeorology00foke/page/n59 42]–49}}</ref>

:<math>
L=-\dfrac{u_*^3}{\kappa \dfrac{g}{\overline{\theta_v}}\overline{w'\theta_v'}}
</math>

The Obukhov length also acts as a criterion for the static stability of surface layer. When <math>L<0</math>, the surface layer is statically unstable, and when <math>L>0</math> the surface layer is statically stable. The [[absolute magnitude]] of <math>L</math> indicates the deviation from statically neutral state, with smaller <math>|L|</math> values corresponding to larger deviations from neutral conditions. When <math>|L|</math> is small and <math>L<0</math>, buoyant processes dominate the production of turbulent kinetic energy compared with shear production. By definition, under neutral conditions <math>L\rightarrow\infty</math>. 
The Obukhov length <math>L</math> is used for non-dimensionalization of height <math>z</math> in similarity theory.

== Governing formulae for similarity relations ==
M–O similarity theory parameterizes fluxes in the surface layer as a function of the dimensionless length parameter <math>\zeta=z/L</math>. From [[Buckingham π theorem|the Buckingham Pi theorem]] of [[dimensional analysis]], two dimensionless group can be formed from the basic parameter set <math>\{ u_*, g/\overline{\theta_v}, \partial\overline{u}/\partial z, z, \overline{w'\theta_v'}\}</math>,

:<math>
\dfrac{\kappa z}{u_*}\dfrac{\partial \overline{u}}{\partial z}
</math>, and 
<math>
\zeta =\dfrac{z}{L}
</math>

From there, a function <math>\varphi_M(\zeta)</math> can be determined to empirically describe the relationship between the two dimensionless quantities, called a universal function. Similarly, <math>\varphi_H(\zeta)</math> can be defined for the dimensionless group of mean temperature profile. 
Mean wind and temperature profiles therefore satisfy the following relations,<ref name = mo54/><ref name = f06/>

:<math>
\dfrac{\partial \overline{u}}{\partial z} =\dfrac{u_*}{\kappa z}\varphi_M(\zeta)
</math>

:<math>
\dfrac{\partial \overline{\theta_v}}{\partial z} =\dfrac{\theta_*}{\kappa z}\varphi_H(\zeta)
</math>

where <math>\theta_*= - \dfrac{\overline{w'\theta_v'}}{u_*}</math> is the characteristic dynamical temperature, <math>\varphi_M</math> and <math>\varphi_H</math> are the universal functions of momentum and heat. The [[Eddy diffusion|eddy diffusivity]] coefficients for momentum and heat fluxes are defined as follows,

:<math>
K_M = \kappa z\dfrac{ u_*}{\varphi_M(\zeta)},\ K_H = \kappa z\dfrac{ u_*}{\varphi_H(\zeta)}
</math>

<math>K_M</math> and <math>K_H</math> can be related with the [[turbulent Prandtl number]] <math>Pr_t</math>,

:<math>
\dfrac{K_H}{K_M}=\dfrac{1}{Pr_t}>1
</math>

In reality, the universal functions need to be determined using experimental data when applying M–O similarity theory. Although the choice of universal functions is not unique, certain functional forms have been proposed and are widely accepted for fitting experimental data.

== Universal functions of the Monin–Obukhov similarity theory ==

[[File:Universal functions for Monin-Obukhov similarity theory.png|thumb|right|500px|Universal functions for Monin–Obukhov similarity theory]]

Several functional forms have been proposed to represent the universal functions of similarity theory. Because the Obukhov length is determined when <math>L\Big(\dfrac{\partial Ri}{\partial z}\Big)_{z=0}=1</math>, where <math>Ri</math> is the [[Richardson number]], the following condition must be satisfied by the universal function chosen,<ref name=mo54/>

:<math>
\varphi(0)=1
</math>

A first order approximation of the universal function for momentum flux is,

:<math>
\varphi_M(\zeta)=1+\beta\zeta
</math>

where <math>\beta\approx 6</math>.<ref name=f06/> However this is only applicable when <math>0<\zeta<1</math>. For conditions where <math>\zeta<0</math>, the relation is,

:<math>
\varphi_M^4-\gamma\zeta\varphi_M^3=1
</math>

where <math>\gamma</math> is a coefficient to be determined from experimental data. This equation can be further approximated by <math>\varphi_M=(1+\gamma\zeta)^{-1/4}</math> when <math>-2<\zeta<0</math>.

Based on the results of the 1968 Kansas experiment, the following universal functions are determined for horizontal mean flow and mean virtual potential temperature,<ref name=b71>{{cite journal|last=Businger|first=J. A.|author-link1=Joost Businger|author2=J. C. Wyngaard |author3=Y. Izumi |author4=E. F. Bradley |title=Flux-profile relationships in the atmospheric surface layer|journal=Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences|date=1971|volume=28|issue=2|pages=181–189|bibcode = 1971JAtS...28..181B |doi = 10.1175/1520-0469(1971)028<0181:FPRITA>2.0.CO;2 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

:<math>
\varphi_M(\zeta)=(1-15\zeta)^{-1/4}\quad -2<\zeta <0
</math>

:<math>
\varphi_M(\zeta)=1+4.7\zeta\quad 0<\zeta <1
</math>

:<math>
\varphi_H(\zeta)=0.74(1-9\zeta)^{-1/2}\quad  -2<\zeta <0
</math>

:<math>
\varphi_H(\zeta)=0.74+4.7\zeta\quad 0<\zeta <1
</math>

Other methods which determine the universal functions using the relation between <math>\zeta</math> and <math>Ri</math> are also used.<ref name=a01>{{cite book|last=Arya|first=S. P.|title=Introduction to Micrometeorology|date=2001|publisher=Academic Press|location=San Diego}}</ref><ref name=h88>{{cite journal|last=Högström|first=U.|title=Non-dimensional wind and temperature profiles in the atmospheric surface layer: A re-evaluation|journal=Boundary-Layer Meteorology|date=1988|volume=42|issue=1–2|pages=55–78|bibcode = 1988BoLMe..42...55H |doi = 10.1007/BF00119875 |s2cid=117742460 }}</ref>

For sublayers with significant roughness, e.g. vegetated surfaces or urban areas, the universal functions must be modified to include the effects of surface roughness.<ref name=f08/>

== Validations ==
A myriad of experimental efforts was devoted to the validation of the M–O similarity theory. Field observations and computer simulations have generally demonstrated that the M–O similarity theory is well satisfied.

=== In field measurements ===
[[File:Rice County P5310407.JPG|350px|thumbnail|right|A Kansas wheat field, the flat terrain is needed for the experiment]]
The 1968 Kansas experiment found great consistency between measurements and predictions from similarity relations for the entire range of stability values.<ref name = b71/> A flat wheat field in Kansas served as the experiment site, with winds measured by anemometers mounted at different heights on a 32 m tower. The temperature profile was also measured in a similar manner. Results from the Kansas field study indicated that the ratio of eddy diffusivities of heat and momentum was approximately 1.35 under neutral conditions. A similar experiment was conducted in a flat field in northwestern Minnesota in 1973. This experiment used both ground and balloon-based observations of the surface layer and further validated the theoretical predictions from similarity.<ref name=k76>{{cite journal|last=Kaimal|first=J. C.|author2=J. C. Wyngaard |author3=D. A. Haugen |author4=O. R. Coté |author5=Y. Izumi |author6=S. J. Caughey |author7=C. J. Readings |title=Turbulence Structure in the Convective Boundary Layer|journal=Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences|date=1976|volume=33|issue=11|pages=2152–2169|bibcode = 1976JAtS...33.2152K |doi = 10.1175/1520-0469(1976)033<2152:TSITCB>2.0.CO;2 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== In large eddy simulations ===
In addition to field experiments, analysis of M–O similarity theory can be conducted using high-resolution [[large eddy simulation]]s. The simulation indicates that the temperature field agrees well with M–O similarity. However, the velocity field shows significant anomalies from M–O similarity.<ref name=les_mo>{{cite journal|last1=Khanna|first1=Samir|last2=Brasseur|first2=James G.|title=Analysis of Monin–Obukhov similarity from large-eddy simulation|journal=J. Fluid Mech.|date=1997|volume=345|issue=1|pages=251–286|doi=10.1017/S0022112097006277|bibcode = 1997JFM...345..251K |s2cid=122546650 }}</ref>

== Limitations ==
M–O similarity theory, albeit successful for surface layers from experimental validations, is essentially a diagnostic empirical theory based upon local first order turbulence closure. Typically, 10%~20% of errors are associated with universal functions. When applied to vegetated areas or complex terrains, it can result in large discrepancies. Because universal functions are often determined under dry conditions, the applicability of M–O similarity theory under moist conditions was not well studied.

The basic parameter set of the M–O similarity theory includes [[buoyancy]] production <math>\dfrac{gQ}{T}</math>. It is argued that with such a parameter set, the scaling is applied to the integral features of the flow, whereas an eddy specific similarity relationship prefers the usage of energy [[dissipation]] rate <math>\epsilon_0</math>.<ref name=m09>{{cite journal|last=McNaughton|first=Keith|title=The rise and fall of Monin-Obukhov theory|journal=AsiaFlux Newsletter|date=2009|issue=30|pages=1–4|url=http://www.mcnaughty.com/keith/papers/Rise_and_Fall_of_MOST.pdf}}</ref> This scheme is able to explain anomalies of M–O similarity theory, but involves non-locality to modeling and experiments.
